name: West Central Oromo
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Gragg, Gene. 1976. Oromo of Wellegga. In Bender (ed.), The Non-Semitic Languages of Ethiopia. (Wellegga = West Central Oromo; not online; Owens 1985 covers Harar, a different variety)

new_statements.quote: Stress and pitch are phonetic in the sense that they are predictable from their phonological environments. [...] There are three stress and or pitch patterns in the dialect of Mecha. Pattern One: A word ending in a short vowel has a primary stress and a high pitch on the penultimate and secondary stress and low pitch on a preceding syllable if there is any. [...] Pattern Two: Any word ending in a consonant or in a long vowel has a primary stress and a high pitch on the ultimate syllable with a secondary stress and a low pitch on any preceding syllable. [...] Pattern Three: In any monosyllabic word, the syllable has a primary stress and a high pitch.
new_statements.citation: Wako Tola. 1981. The Phonology of Mecha Oromo. MA thesis, Addis Ababa University, School of Graduate Studies. Section 4.3 'Stress and Pitch', 4.3.1 'Patterns of Stress and Pitch'.
new_statements.locator: pp. 44-46 (quote from pp. 44-46; PDF pp. 50-52); dialect basis p. 1; summary p. 70
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress (realised as high pitch) falls on the final syllable when it is heavy (closed or long-vowelled: bisá:n 'water', matá: 'head', dè:mán 'they went'), otherwise on the penultimate (náma 'person', barbá:de 'wanted', galgála 'evening'); monosyllables are stressed. Stress is predictable, not lexically contrastive, but shifts carry grammatical meaning (e.g. imperative vs non-finite verb, affirmative vs negative hin-).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress (with low pitch) on a syllable preceding the primary one 'if there is any' (Wako 1981: 45-46); Dejene 2010: 45-46 (Wello) locates it on the antepenult in penult-stressed polysyllables and on the penult (or a non-final long-vowel syllable) in final-stressed words.
new_statements.exceptions: Grammatically conditioned shifts: verbal adjectives take primary stress on both ultimate and penultimate; non-finite verb forms and yes/no-question infinitives take secondary on the penult and primary on the ultimate; imperatives primary on the penult; prefix hin- primary-stressed = affirmative, secondary-stressed = negative (pp. 46-48). Dejene 2010: 46 adds that open monosyllabic clitics (tu, nu, na, si) are unstressed and that in consonant-final words a non-final long-vowel syllable takes the primary stress (áatàm 'sixty', torbáatàm 'seventy').
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level citation forms of the Mecha dialect (Leka variety around Nekemte); the author analyses the language as a stress language with pitch as the main correlate (three degrees of stress, two pitch levels; note 21: 'no separate stress or pitch' found at this level). This is contested: Habte Bulti 2003 (Macha of Jimma/Nedjo/Ambo) analyses the same variety as tonal and calls stress 'contextually motivated'; Dejene Geshe 2010 (Wello) defends the stress analysis and reports the same placement pattern.
new_statements.identity_note: Wako Tola 1981 describes the Mecha (Macha/Wellega) dialect, specifically the Leka variety around Nekemte; Mecha is a dialect child of west2721 in Glottolog (the same dialect basis as the scan-named Gragg 1976 'Oromo of Wellegga'). Corroborating first-hand description Dejene Geshe 2010 is for Kamisee = Wello (Glottolog well1239, also under west2721). Habte Bulti 2003 (Macha of Jimma/Nedjo/Ambo) is the same language but a tonal analysis. Tilahun Gamta 1999 and Hodson & Walker 1922 do not specify a single dialect. Harar (east2652) and Borana/Orma/Waata sources were not used.

sources.locator: pp. 44-46 (quote from pp. 44-46; PDF pp. 50-52); dialect basis p. 1; summary p. 70
sources.note: Sec. 4.3 'Stress and Pitch' pp. 44-46: three degrees of stress, two pitch levels, primary stress and high pitch coincide; stress/pitch 'phonetic... predictable from their phonological environments', grammatical but not lexical. Pattern One: word ending in a short vowel -> primary stress on the penultimate; Pattern Two: word ending in a consonant or a long vowel -> primary stress on the ultimate; Pattern Three: monosyllables stressed. Dialect basis: Mecha of Leka around Nekemte (p. 1).

sources.citation: Dejene Geshe. 2010. Kamisee Oromo Phonology. MA thesis, Addis Ababa University. 81 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 5.3-5.3.1 pp. 44-47 (Wello/Kamisee dialect = Glottolog well1239 under west2721): three degrees of stress marked mainly by pitch; disyllables ending in a short vowel and polysyllables without long vowels -> primary stress penultimate; words ending in a long vowel or a consonant -> primary stress ultimate (a non-final long-vowel syllable takes it instead in consonant-final words); monosyllables stressed except clitics tu, nu, na, si; 'stress is phonetic... no lexical contrast' (p. 44); 'Kamisee Oromo is a stress language with a dynamic placement of the stress based on the pitch movement an…

sources.citation: Habte Bulti. 2003. Analysis of Tone in Oromo. MA thesis, Addis Ababa University.
sources.note: Macha dialect of Jimma, Nedjo and Ambo (p. 3). Treats Oromo as tonal; pp. 17-18: reports Lloret 1988 (primary stress on the penultimate of nouns in base form) and Abera 1988: 32; own observation that syllables before geminates and with long vowels are more prominent and that focus answers stress the initial syllable, concluding 'the occurrence of stress is contextually motivated and its assignment has no influence over and joint function with tone' (p. 18). Rejects Wako 1981's link of high tone to primary stress (p. 10).

sources.citation: Tilahun Gamta (Xilaahun Gamtaa). 1999. Structural and word stress patterns in Afaan Oromo. Journal of Oromo Studies 6(1-2): 173-194.
sources.note: Sec. 3.2 pp. 187-189, rules 'based on the writer's idiolect', dialect not named: words whose final vowel is short -a stress the first syllable (Rules 1-3: MA.na, GA.nna, GAL.ma); words ending in any other vowel stress the second syllable (Rules 4-6: bi.TAA, bo.KKAA); 'stress should be understood to mean a relative syllable strength that depends on the quality and quantity of the vowel' (p. 187).

sources.citation: Hodson, Arnold W. & Craven H. Walker. 1922. An Elementary and Practical Grammar of the Galla or Oromo Language. London: SPCK.
sources.note: Sec. 8 pp. 12-13: 'In the vast majority of cases the tonic accent will be found to fall on the penultimate syllable'; oxytone/proparoxytone words marked with an acute; enclitic demonstratives throw the accent onto the final syllable of the preceding word (sec. 9). Composite dialect basis (Walker at Gore in western Oromo territory, Hodson at Mega in Borana).
